transcript.text: LG F4V5VYP0W says OE and the clothes are sat in water. I'm not opening the little door at the bottom because last time I did that it flooded the whole kitchen. What else can I do?

OE on an LG means the machine tried to pump out for around 13 minutes and the water level didn't drop. The usual causes are, most likely first: a blocked pump filter (coins, hair grips, fluff), a kinked drain hose or a blocked standpipe or sink waste, and less often a jammed or failed drain pump. The flood last time probably happened because the filter was opened with a full drum behind it. A whole drum of water comes out fast. 1. Check the drain hose and waste first. You can do this without touching the filter. Pull the machine out a little and look for a kink or crush in the grey hose behind it. If it runs into a sink waste, check the sink drains properly. A blocked trap, or a new sink fitted with the blanking cap still in the spigot, gives exactly this code. If you find and clear something here, try step 2 again.
2. Run a Spin or Drain-only programme and listen low down at the front. If the water goes away, the hose or waste was the problem. If the pump hums or rattles but no water moves, it's probably a blockage at the filter or pump. If it's completely silent, the pump itself becomes more likely.
3. Use the small emergency drain tube if your machine has one. Most LG front-loaders have a thin rubber tube with a plug, behind the same bottom flap next to the round filter cap. Switch off and unplug the machine and lay towels down. Pull the tube out, hold it over a baking tray or shallow container, and remove its little plug. The water only trickles out, so you can stop it at any time by putting the plug back while you empty the tray. It's slow, but there's no flood. 4. Only then open the filter, with a towel and tray underneath, unscrewing it slowly so the last cupful comes out gently. Clear out whatever is in it, check the impeller behind it turns, and screw the cap back in fully and straight. If there's no emergency tube, the controlled way is to loosen the filter cap only a quarter turn so it trickles into the tray, then tighten it, empty the tray and repeat. If the filter and hose are both clear and it still shows OE, especially with a silent or humming pump, that points to the drain pump. At that stage an engineer is a sensible option. What happens when you try a Spin/Drain-only programme?
Ok, the machine was pushed right back against the wall and the hose was squashed behind it. I've pulled it out and straightened it. I'll try the spin again now.

That's a very likely culprit. A drain hose crushed against the wall is one of the most common causes of OE, because the pump simply can't push water past the squash. Machines that get nudged back during spinning often end up like this. While you run the spin, here's what each result would mean: 1. If the water pumps away and it spins normally, the hose was the problem. Run a quick Rinse and Spin so the clothes aren't left soggy. When you push the machine back, leave a hand's width gap behind it, and check the hose runs in a smooth curve without being pinched. If it has a sharp crease from being squashed, it may kink again in the same spot. A replacement drain hose is cheap and easy to fit if so.
2. If the water drains but slowly, the hose may have been only part of it. There may also be some fluff or debris building up in the pump filter, so it's worth a controlled filter clean later using the emergency tube method I described.
3. If it still shows OE and you hear the pump humming but no water moves, there's probably a blockage at the filter or pump as well. The trickle-drain route keeps the floor dry.
4. If it's completely silent when it should be pumping, the drain pump itself becomes the more likely cause. Let me know what happens.
Tried it. It drained a little slower than normal and then OE came up again. Still not touching that filter though.

Before you start, switch it off and unplug it. It now drains, just too slowly, so it still trips OE (the machine gives up if the level hasn't dropped in time). A slow drain like this usually means something is still partly in the way. The most likely spot is the pump filter, with fluff or a small object narrowing the flow. The next most likely is the rest of the drain path: a crease left where the hose was crushed, or a partly blocked standpipe or sink trap. A tired pump is less likely. 1. Look at the hose where it was crushed. If it has a flat, creased section that won't round out, it can still pinch. A new drain hose is cheap and simple to fit.
2. Check where the hose ends. If it goes into a standpipe, it should only go in about 15cm. Pushed down too far, it can restrict the flow. If it goes into a sink waste, run the sink tap hard for a minute. If the sink is slow to clear, the trap or waste is part of the problem.
3. Do a bucket test. This tells the machine apart from your plumbing, and it's controllable. Unhook the hose from the standpipe or sink end only, and hold the end in a bucket at about worktop height. Run Spin. If the water gushes out strongly, the machine is fine and your waste plumbing is the restriction. If it only dribbles, the blockage is inside the machine, at the filter or pump. Keep the hose end held high and the flow stops as soon as the pump stops, so you won't get a flood. Don't lower the end to the floor, because it can then siphon the whole drum out by gravity. If the bucket test shows a weak flow, then the filter really is the next step. If you'd rather not open it yourself, that's completely reasonable. An engineer can drain it under control, clear the filter and check the pump in one visit. It's usually a quick, inexpensive job if it's only a blockage. Where does your hose go, and how strong is the flow in the bucket?
The kitchen sink drains fine. I'm not sure about the bucket test though, I don't want water going all over my laminate. Is there anything else I can try that's safer?

Yes, there's a safer version that keeps the floor dry. A sink that drains well is a good sign, but it doesn't rule out the waste connection. The spigot on the trap that the machine hose pushes onto can clog with lint even when the sink itself runs freely. So there are still two likely spots: inside the machine at the filter or pump (most likely), or that hose-to-waste connection. 1. Do the flow test into the sink instead of a bucket. Switch off at the plug, lay a towel under the sink and put a bowl in the cupboard under the connection. Pull the hose off the waste spigot or standpipe. Only the water already in the hose will come out. Bring the hose end up and hook it firmly over the rim of the empty sink, held with a peg or tied loosely to the tap so it can't jump out. Plug back in and run Spin. The sink easily takes the whole drumful, and the end stays high, so it can't siphon. A strong, steady gush means the machine is pumping fine and the restriction is the waste spigot. A weak dribble means the problem is inside the machine.
2. Poke a finger or the handle of a teaspoon into it. If it's furred up with lint or gunk, clear it. On a newer trap, make sure the inner blanking membrane has been fully cut out. A partly blocked spigot gives exactly this slow drain.
3. Run your hand along the hose where it was crushed. If there's a flat, creased section that won't round out, a new drain hose is cheap and pushes straight on. If the flow test gives only a dribble, the restriction is at the filter or pump. Since you'd rather not open the filter, which is completely fair after last time, that's the point to book an engineer. They can drain it under control, clear the filter and check the pump in one visit. If it's just a blockage, it's usually a quick job. Don't open the drum door until the water level is below the glass. What's the flow like when it goes into the sink?

I'm still nervous about unhooking the hose, to be honest. My husband can sort the filter at the weekend. Is it safe to leave it till then, and is there a way to get the water out without opening the filter?

Yes, it's safe to leave it until the weekend. Water sitting in the drum won't harm the machine. Switch it off at the plug in the meantime and keep the hose straight. The main downside is the clothes. Left sitting in water for several days they'll start to smell and can pick up mildew spots, so it's worth getting them out if you can. You can get the water out without opening the filter, and without unhooking anything: 1. Run Spin (or Drain) again, two or three times. It is draining, just too slowly. Each run should still pump some water away before OE comes up. Switch off between goes, then start again. A few runs like this won't hurt the pump. Once the water is below the bottom of the door glass, the door should unlock after a minute or two. Lift the clothes out, give them a wring over the sink and rewash them once the machine's sorted. If the level isn't visibly dropping after a couple of tries, stop and leave it for the weekend.
2. Leave the emergency drain tube for your husband. It's the slow, controllable option I described earlier, and it's the best way to empty whatever's left before he opens the filter. For the weekend, the filter is still the most likely culprit. A slow drain after the hose was freed usually means fluff or a small object is narrowing the pump inlet. When he does it, these are worth passing on: 1. Drain through the emergency tube into a tray first, with towels down. Only open the filter once it's down to a trickle, unscrewing it slowly.
2. Clear the filter, shine a torch in and check the impeller behind it turns freely.
3. Screw the cap back in fully and straight.
4. While he's at it, check the spigot on the sink trap where the machine hose pushes on. It can fur up with lint even when the sink drains fine. Also run a hand along the hose where it was crushed, feeling for a flat crease that won't round out. If the filter and those connections are all clear and it still drains slowly with OE, the drain pump becomes the likely cause. That's the point to get an engineer in. Does a couple of Spin runs get the water below the door glass?
